rationale: B wins because it separates the actual sellable human story from the broader category take. A's "Discord opens a paid tier inside community servers built on free membership" is a decent trend wrapper, but B's "What a gaming-community server can now charge for, and what stays free" gives a founder the story a reporter can actually report: one named server, pricing, gating, and what remains free. A is strong, but it casually imports context like "Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers" that was not in the update; B is more disciplined about refusing unsupported competitor and backlash pegs.
gaps_in_A: "Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers" imports outside comparator facts that were not in the update. Useful context, yes; still unsupported in a blind angle set.
"Discord servers have historically been free communities" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts. Don't smuggle background knowledge in as a premise.
The third kept angle stays at trend altitude. It asks for "a named server owner" as proof, but never makes the named server owner a separate customer-story angle.

"Discord priced its cut at a third of the app-store standard and is making the take rate the pitch" overstates intent. The facts give the 10% vs. 30% contrast; they do not prove Discord is deliberately making that the pitch.
gaps_in_B: "the fee comparison is Discord's own framing" is not established by the update. The comparison is supplied as a fact, but not necessarily as Discord's message.
"The launch lands while the IPO reporting is live" is a little too confident. The update says reportedly preparing for an IPO, not that there is live current reporting this week.

"early subscriber counts" in the customer-story proof is directionally right, but the update says no creator-earnings data exists yet. Ask for pricing and setup first; don't make counts the floor too early.
"can a private community be the product" is a nice line, but it needs external examples or data before it becomes more than a clever wrapper.
